name: Erlang
summary: A dynamically typed functional language from Ericsson, built for systems that must never stop: lightweight processes that share nothing, supervisors that restart what fails, and code that can be upgraded while it runs.
intro: Erlang is a functional language whose variables are bound by pattern matching, and whose unit of concurrency is the process: a lightweight process owned by the runtime, not the operating system. Processes share no memory and talk only by sending messages, which the receiver picks out of its mailbox with `receive` and patterns. When a process dies, it sends an exit signal to the processes linked to it, so failures are handled by other processes instead of with defensive code at every step. Erlang/OTP, the distribution, turns that into structure: supervisors are processes that watch workers and restart them, arranged in supervision trees, and behaviours such as `gen_server` and `supervisor` supply the generic half of common process types so you write only the callbacks.

The compiler `erlc` produces `.beam` files that run on BEAM, the Erlang virtual machine, which schedules processes preemptively across all cores, collects each process’s heap separately and can load a new version of a module while the old one is still running. Several Erlang runtimes on different machines can be joined into a cluster of nodes, and sending a message to a process on another node looks the same as sending one locally. Types are checked at run time; Dialyzer, a static analysis tool shipped with Erlang/OTP, finds definite type errors and unreachable code.
strengths: Concurrency is the core of the language: a new process costs 327 words, so one per call, connection or device is normal
Fault tolerance by design: links, exit signals and supervision trees restart failed parts instead of letting errors spread
Hot code loading and built-in distribution, both part of the language and runtime rather than add-on libraries
Decades of production use in telecom, with OTP behaviours that encode proven patterns for servers, state machines and supervisors
limits: Dynamic typing: type errors surface at run time unless you run Dialyzer, which reports only errors it can prove
Messages are copied between processes, so sharing large data structures between processes is expensive
Number crunching is not its strength: BeamAsm translates instruction by instruction with hardly any optimisation across them

story: Erlang started in 1986 at the Ericsson Computer Science Laboratory with one goal: “to provide a better way of programming telephony applications.” A switch handles tens or hundreds of thousands of calls at once, must keep working when parts fail, and must be upgraded without being switched off. The first version was an interpreter written in Prolog, which is where its dynamic typing comes from. In 1989 Joe Armstrong, Robert Virding and Mike Williams built JAM, a virtual machine about 70 times faster.

Ericsson formed a product unit, OTP (Open Telecom Platform), to support Erlang; it shipped the first Erlang/OTP release in 1996 and became a separate unit in 1997. The AXD301 switch, announced in March 1998, was possibly the largest program ever written in a functional language. Yet in February 1998 Ericsson Radio banned Erlang for new products. That ban led indirectly to Open Source Erlang in December 1998, after which most of the original team left to found Bluetail, and Erlang began spreading outside Ericsson.

choices.choice: Processes in the language, not the operating system
choices.why: Telephone systems are concurrent by nature. Making processes lightweight and part of the language, a minority view at the time, let programs model each call or device as its own process.

Error recovery is impossible if the data needed for it sits on a machine that has crashed. Every process keeps enough local information to carry on when another part fails, and mutexes over shared data were too hard to get right in a distributed system.

A fault-tolerant system needs at least two computers that watch each other, because the one that failed can’t repair itself. Erlang applied the same idea inside a program: a dying process sends an exit signal to linked processes, which recover for it.
Erlang started life as a Prolog interpreter and kept a dynamic type system. Later attempts to add static typing proved very hard, so checking was left to optional tools such as Dialyzer.
